name: Felix Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or parties, and your name won't appear in our findings. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Felix Evans, 58, a junior operator at a big mine outside town. I check the haul truck before dawn, move broken rock to the crusher, and radio the control room when the grade changes; the cab shakes my knees by lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What parts do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a clean run of trucks reach the crusher without a hold-up. The dust gets into everything, and my partner Ruth says I come home still listening for the radio, even when it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the mine still runs on diesel and maintenance, not headlines. The small software changes might tidy the dispatch board, but my shift and pay look much the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the system only handles routine routing, it won’t replace the judgement I use when a truck sounds wrong. I still don’t want to learn software for its own sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my usual shift and continue paying our household bills from my wage. I’d ask the pension office for a current estimate this winter, because I don’t know the exact figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, though retirement planning still sits in the **back of my mind**. I can live with that for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the mine added a routing screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d let Martin explain it at the toolbox talk and use it only after a clear demonstration. I wouldn’t volunteer to be the first one experimenting while trucks are moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household expense would you change first if your hours dipped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d pause the shed repairs and keep the heating and food budget intact. Ruth and I would talk before using the savings we’ve built over years.

say: I’d tell the crew **diesel and maintenance** still run this mine.
I’d say the **dispatch board** may improve, while our shifts and pay stay much the same.
think: I trust my **truck judgement** when a machine sounds wrong.
I don’t want **software lessons** for their own sake.
do: Keep my **usual shift** and pay the household bills from my wage.
Ask the **pension office** for a current estimate this winter.
Watch Martin demonstrate the **routing screen** before using it.
feel: I feel **relieved** that the mine still needs me.
S0.quote: I’d keep my usual shift and continue paying our household bills from my wage.
fieldNote: His relief rests on a clear distinction between **routine routing** and hearing trouble in a truck.
He wants **Martin’s demonstration** before touching a new screen during live work.
The pension estimate reflects an **existing worry**, even in a mild AI picture.

steps.text: Keep driving the usual haul truck shift and paying household bills from wages
Wait for Martin’s toolbox demonstration before using the new routing screen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that planning screens may get smarter while the road still needs a person at the wheel. The company should explain any change to shifts before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That may only buy time: the mine could reduce the crew before robots arrive. I don’t like new systems and would need someone beside me, not a login and a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get my pension estimate and ask HR what happens to it if I leave at 60. I’d practise the mine’s screen-based dispatch with a patient coworker, rather than sign up for a broad course I may not finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: **Worried**, but not expecting a layoff tomorrow. I can live with that for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children after a shift where a planning screen replaced a control-room task?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them the control room has fewer routine calls, but I still drove my assigned truck that day. I’d ask them not to treat one quiet week as proof the whole mine is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about first if the company cut a crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d worry about the youngest temporary drivers first, because they have less time in the mine and less say. I’d worry about myself too if the cuts reached junior operators.

say: I’d say **smarter planning screens** still leave drivers on the haul road.
I’d ask the company to explain **shift changes** before they arrive.
think: I worry the mine could **shrink crews** before robots appear.
I’d need a **coworker beside me**, because a login and leaflet would leave me stuck.
do: Get a **pension estimate** and ask HR what leaving at 60 would mean.
Practise **screen dispatch** with a patient coworker during a mine shift.
feel: I feel **worried** about junior operators facing cuts.
S1.quote: I’d tell the crew that planning screens may get smarter while the road still needs a person at the wheel.
fieldNote: He publicly stresses the **driver’s seat**, while privately allowing for earlier crew reductions.
His own **junior standing** makes cuts personal after he mentions temporary drivers.
He prefers **one coworker’s help** to a broad course he doubts he would finish.

steps.text: Practise the mine’s screen dispatch with a patient coworker during a shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that thinking AI may take the control-room planning in 2028, while hands-on robots are expected around 2031. Nobody should pretend those dates leave us prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m 58 now and would be 60 when AGI arrives, but I can’t count on a pension starting exactly when I need it. I don’t use AI and don’t trust myself to learn it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the pension office for a written estimate and request HR explain what happens if my job ends in 2028 or 2031. I’d keep applying only to nearby equipment jobs that list my experience, and discuss retirement timing with Ruth before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m **scared of the gap** between a final shift and pension eligibility. I can live with that for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exact bill would you cut first if your pay stopped in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d stop the shed repair and reduce meals out straight away. The mortgage is paid, but utilities and groceries still come every month, so I’d need a bridge income quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try another job outside mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d look at equipment work nearby, but I’m slow with new systems and wouldn’t claim I can do a technical desk job. I’d need a real vacancy and a wage we could live on.

say: I’d tell the crew **2028 AI** and **2031 robots** leave little time to prepare.
I’d say nobody should pretend the mine is **ready**.
think: I could be **60** when planning work changes, without a pension I can draw.
I cannot learn unfamiliar **AI alone** or count on a desk job.
do: Request a **written pension estimate** and HR’s figures for losing work in 2028 or 2031.
Apply for **nearby equipment jobs** that fit my experience.
Discuss **retirement timing** with Ruth before signing anything.
feel: I’m **scared** of a gap between my final shift and pension eligibility.
I need **bridge income** if pay stops.
S2.quote: I’m 58 now and would be 60 when AGI arrives, but I can’t count on a pension starting exactly when I need it.
fieldNote: The **2028 date** frightens him through pension eligibility, even though physical robots follow in 2031.
He rules out a **technical desk job** and limits applications to equipment vacancies nearby.
He names **shed repairs** and meals out as first cuts if wages stop.

steps.text: Apply for nearby equipment vacancies that ask for his mine driving experience
Stop shed repairs and reduce meals out if mine pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives the mine time to speak plainly about planning software in 2031 and robots around 2034. I’d want older operators included in decisions, not told at the last safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use the years to make a decision, but I may still be short of pension age when the physical work goes. I don’t want to gamble our reserve on retraining that leads nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the pension office to compare leaving at 60, 63 and 65. I’d set a date with Ruth to review that estimate each January, then apply only for local equipment jobs if the mine starts cutting shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel **cautious**, with more room to choose than in the two-year picture. I can live with that for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a training offer from the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d trust it if an operator could practise on paid shifts with an instructor and the union could see the job plan. A classroom link after a twelve-hour shift wouldn’t persuade me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years make you sell anything or move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our home is paid for and close to Ruth’s family. I’d rather discuss the pension and local work before we considered moving away.

say: I’d say five years gives the mine time to explain **2031 software** and **2034 robots**.
I’d insist **older operators** be included before the last safety meeting.
think: I may still fall short of **pension age** when physical jobs go.
I won’t gamble our **savings reserve** on uncertain retraining.
do: Ask the pension office to compare leaving at **60, 63 and 65**.
Review the estimate with **Ruth each January**.
Apply for **local equipment work** if mine shifts are cut.
feel: I feel **cautious**, with more room to choose than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: I can use the years to make a decision, but I may still be short of pension age when the physical work goes.
fieldNote: The extra years let him compare **three retirement ages**, but do not settle the pension gap.
He would trust training on **paid shifts** with an instructor and union visibility.
He rejects moving because the **paid-off home** is close to Ruth’s family.

steps.text: Apply for local equipment jobs if the mine starts cutting shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that ten years is enough time to plan carefully, but full thinking AI in 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039 still change this line of work. The company should start talking while there’s time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There may be time for me to retire before 2039, but the 2036 planning change could affect shifts earlier. I don’t want the company to treat age as proof that I have no bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare pension options by 2028 and make a retirement plan by 2032 with my partner Ruth. If the mine cuts my hours after 2036, I’d ask HR about bridge income before drawing savings down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel **more in control**, not certain. I can live with that for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most if the company announced a robot schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want a written timeline, my pension estimate, and a union representative in the same meeting. A clear bridge payment would matter more than a promise that someone might hire me elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask how the work wears people down before asking whether they can learn another system. My knees and the noise are part of why I need a realistic retirement plan.

say: I’d say a decade permits **careful planning**, though 2036 AI and 2039 robots still change mining.
I’d ask the company to start **talking now**.
think: I may **retire before 2039**, if pension figures allow it.
I still have **bills** if planning changes reduce shifts in 2036.
do: Compare **pension options** by 2028 and plan retirement with Ruth by 2032.
Ask HR about **bridge income** if the mine cuts hours after 2036.
feel: I feel **more in control**, though the outcome remains uncertain.
S4.quote: I’d tell the crew that ten years is enough time to plan carefully, but full thinking AI in 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039 still change this line of work.
fieldNote: The longer horizon makes **retirement before robots** possible without guaranteeing income until then.
He wants a **written timeline**, pension estimate and union representative in one meeting.
His **knees and noise exposure** make retirement planning about health as well as machines.

steps.text: Keep working mine shifts while comparing pension options by 2028

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose my shift before my pension starts. A written pension estimate and a bridge payment for older operators would help me make a real choice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company gives people paid time to learn a changed screen. A man my age can learn when someone shows him patiently, but I won’t pretend an online course after a dusty shift is easy.

headlineQuote: I’d compare pension options by 2028 and make a retirement plan by 2032 with my partner Ruth.
portrait: Felix Evans, 58, is a **junior haul truck operator** at a large mine, with aching knees after dusty shifts.
He and **partner Ruth** have grown children, a paid-off home and savings covering one to six months.
He avoids **AI tools**, but will learn a dispatch screen through patient help on a paid shift.
Faster change threatens his **pension bridge**; a decade could let him retire before hands-on robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because he could lose shifts before his pension begins.
whatWouldHelp: A **written pension estimate** and bridge payment for older operators would let him choose a realistic retirement date.
He also needs **paid instruction** from a patient coworker when the mine changes its screens.
